question: Electrical bonding of an aircraft means:

options.text: Joining all metal parts with low-resistance paths so they share one potential
Connecting the aircraft to the earth with a lead whenever it is parked
Insulating every metal part from every other to prevent current flowing between them
Wrapping cables in a metal braid to stop radio interference

explanation: Bonding makes the aircraft a single, continuous conductor. Wrapping cables in braid is screening, a related but different measure; connecting to earth on the ground is grounding.

question: Which of the following is a purpose of bonding?

options.text: Raising the potential of the control surfaces above that of the structure
Storing static charge in the structure for later discharge
Increasing the resistance between the engine and the airframe
Preventing sparks between parts, providing the earth return and carrying lightning current

explanation: Parts at different potentials can spark — a serious hazard near fuel. Bonding also provides the low-resistance return for single-pole circuits, conducts lightning current through the structure without arcing at joints, and reduces radio interference.

question: Bonding jumpers (flexible straps) are fitted across hinges of control surfaces and across engine mountings because:

options.text: The straps carry the hydraulic pressure across the joint
Hinges and rubber mounts do not conduct reliably on their own
They are needed only to carry the radio aerial signal
They limit the movement of the control surface

explanation: Bearings are lubricated, mountings are often rubber, and joints may be painted or anodised — any of which can insulate one part from another. Flexible jumpers keep the electrical path intact while allowing movement.

question: A poor (high-resistance) bond between two parts of the structure can lead to:

options.text: Improved lightning protection, because current is kept out of the joint
A higher generator output voltage
Arcing at the joint, and radio interference
Lower fuel consumption, because less static is generated

explanation: Current always finds a path. If the bond is poor, it may jump across the joint as an arc — a fire hazard near fuel and a source of electrical noise.

question: An aircraft in flight builds up static electricity mainly through:

options.text: Leakage of current from the generators into the structure
Induction from the aircraft's own radio transmitters
Friction with precipitation and dust (triboelectric charging)
The magnetic field of the Earth acting on the moving structure

explanation: Charge is transferred when particles strike the airframe. The build-up can reach high potentials, especially in precipitation, and then discharges from points and edges into the surrounding air.

question: Precipitation static ('P-static') discharging from an aircraft causes:

options.text: A loss of engine power by ionising the intake air
Overcharging of the aircraft battery
Radio noise, especially on low-frequency receivers such as the ADF
Errors in the magnetic compass caused by the discharge current

explanation: Corona discharge from sharp extremities creates broadband electrical noise. Lower frequencies suffer most, and the ADF's needle can wander or the receiver may become unusable in heavy precipitation.

question: Static dischargers (static wicks) fitted to the trailing edges of the wings and tail surfaces are designed to:

options.text: Bleed static charge gently into the air, reducing radio noise
Increase the build-up of static charge for de-icing purposes
Conduct lightning strikes safely from the aircraft to the air
Earth the aircraft to the ground during refuelling

explanation: Dischargers bleed charge at a low current from many points at the trailing edges, where discharge happens anyway, and in a way that generates less radio noise. They are not designed for lightning currents and may be damaged by a strike.

question: Several static wicks are found missing during a walk-round. A likely consequence in flight is:

options.text: Loss of lightning protection for the whole aircraft
Increased fuel consumption from the extra drag
More radio interference when flying through precipitation
Failure of the generator to come on line

explanation: With fewer dischargers, static leaves the airframe in a less controlled way, causing more noise. The minimum number required is set in the aircraft's maintenance and dispatch documents.

question: Before refuelling begins, a bonding lead is connected between the aircraft and the fuel truck or hydrant cart. Its purpose is to:

options.text: Equalise their potentials so no spark can jump between them
Earth the aircraft so its battery cannot discharge during refuelling
Allow the fuel quantity indication to work during refuelling
Carry electrical power from the truck to the aircraft's refuel panel

explanation: Fuel flowing through hoses and filters generates static, and the aircraft and the vehicle may already be at different potentials. Bonding them first — before the hose is connected or the tank opened — removes the spark risk in the presence of fuel vapour.

question: On the ground, the static charge on a parked aircraft is commonly dissipated by:

options.text: Conductive tyres and/or a static earthing (grounding) lead
Switching the battery off, which removes the charge
The static wicks, which work as well on the ground as in flight
Running the APU, which neutralises the charge

explanation: Tyres containing conductive material and earthing leads to ground points let accumulated charge flow away into the ground. Static wicks need airflow to work effectively.

question: Lightning typically attaches to an aircraft at:

options.text: Extremities such as the nose, wingtips and tail
The centre of the fuselage, where the skin is thickest
Only the static wicks, which are designed to attract it
The landing gear, which is always the first point of contact

explanation: The strike attaches where the electric field is strongest — protruding points and edges — and the current flows through the conducting skin to an exit point. Because the aircraft moves, the attachment can 'sweep' back along the surface.

question: A conventional metal aircraft protects its occupants from a lightning strike mainly because:

options.text: The current passes through the electrical system to the battery, which absorbs it
The tyres insulate the aircraft from the lightning path
The static wicks absorb the energy of the strike
The metal skin carries the current around the outside, like a Faraday cage

explanation: A closed conducting shell keeps the current on its outer surface. Bonding ensures the current crosses joints without arcing. That is why lightning rarely harms people inside, though it can damage avionics and leave burn marks at attachment points.

question: Composite structures need special provision against lightning, such as embedded metal mesh or foil, because:

options.text: Composite parts are never inspected after a lightning strike
Composites conduct poorly, so a strike could damage them and the wiring inside
Composites attract lightning far more strongly than aluminium does
Composites cannot be bonded to metal parts by any means

explanation: Without a good conducting path, lightning current can burn through a composite skin or arc within it, and the reduced shielding allows strong fields to induce surges in nearby cables. Mesh, foil and conducting strips restore a path for the current.

question: A radome (nose cone) of non-conducting material is protected from lightning by:

options.text: Earthing the weather radar antenna to the battery negative
Static wicks mounted inside the radome
Painting it with an insulating coating
Diverter strips that conduct strike current to the structure

explanation: The radome must let radar energy through, so it cannot be metal. Segmented or solid diverter strips on its surface give the strike a path to the airframe without blocking the radar.

question: Screening (shielding) of cables, by surrounding the conductors with a metal braid, is done to:

options.text: Protect the cable insulation from fluids
Stop the cable radiating or picking up interference
Provide the earth return for the circuit in place of bonding
Increase the current-carrying capacity of the cable

explanation: An earthed braid intercepts electric and electromagnetic fields. Sensitive signal cables (radio, sensors) are screened to keep noise out, and noisy circuits are screened to keep it in.

question: Signal wires are often twisted together in pairs because:

options.text: Twisting increases the wire's current rating
Twisted wires do not need any insulation
Twisting makes the pair act as a capacitor that stores charge
Interference induced in the two wires is nearly equal and cancels

explanation: Each twist swaps the wires' positions relative to a nearby field, so the voltages induced in them are nearly equal and cancel in a differential circuit.

question: HIRF (High Intensity Radiated Fields) is a concern for modern aircraft because:

options.text: It affects only the magnetic compass and nothing else on board
Strong transmitter fields can induce currents that disrupt electronics
Fields from the aircraft's own generators heat the cabin structure
It is produced by the static wicks during lightning strikes

explanation: Digital avionics and fly-by-wire systems must keep working when flying past powerful transmitters. Certification requires HIRF protection through screening, bonding, filtering and system design.

question: Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) means that equipment:

options.text: Can be connected to any busbar without circuit protection
Works properly in its environment without disturbing other equipment
Operates on both AC and DC supplies interchangeably
Is magnetically shielded so that it cannot be affected by any field

explanation: EMC covers both sides: emission (what a device puts out) and susceptibility (what it can tolerate). Bonding, screening, filtering and wiring separation together achieve it.

question: Passengers may be asked to switch off or set portable electronic devices to flight mode during critical phases because:

options.text: They discharge the aircraft's static wicks
They could interfere with communication and navigation equipment
They attract lightning to the passenger cabin
They draw power from the aircraft's electrical system through the seat

explanation: Transmitting devices radiate on frequencies that could couple into aircraft wiring or receivers. Rules for what is allowed depend on the aircraft and the operator, which is why they vary.

question: The resistance of a bond between two major structural parts should be:

options.text: Equal to the resistance of the cables in the circuits nearby
As high as possible, to stop any current flowing between the parts
Unimportant, provided the parts touch each other physically
Very low — milliohms — so large currents cause no harmful voltage or heat

explanation: A bond must carry large currents with almost no voltage drop. Maintenance checks measure bonding resistance with a low-resistance ohmmeter against limits of milliohms set by the manufacturer.

question: Bonding strips must be fitted to clean metal, free of paint, anodising and grease, because:

options.text: Paint makes the strip too rigid to allow the joint to move
Grease conducts static charge away before it can build up
Any insulating film adds resistance and invites corrosion at the joint
Anodising increases the strip's current rating too far

explanation: A bond only works if it has a very low resistance. Coatings and oxides insulate, and dissimilar metals in poor contact corrode electrolytically, raising the resistance further over time.

question: Which kind of equipment most needs screening to prevent radio interference?

options.text: Equipment that makes and breaks a circuit rapidly, such as commutator machines and ignition systems
Batteries, because the chemical action in their cells radiates radio noise
Bonding strips, because the static charge they carry interferes with radios
Purely resistive heaters fed with a steady direct current from the bus

explanation: Sparking brushes, ignition and any device switching a circuit many times a second generate broadband electrical noise. Suppressors and a continuous metal sheath around their cables keep that noise out of the radios.
